Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed post-hoc biomarker analysis of phase 3 trial data•October 16, 2026

Baseline amyloid burden predicts one-year donanemab PET clearance

In a TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 post-hoc analysis, lower baseline amyloid was the strongest predictor of reaching less than 24.1 Centiloids at week 52; amyloid-clear and non-clear subgroups had similar CDR-SB slowing, while tau-PET slowing was significant only after clearance.

Key quantitative results: Among evaluable donanemab-treated participants, 443 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids at week 52 and 227 did not. Mean baseline amyloid was 95.8 versus 120.2 Centiloids; week-52 means were 4.8 versus 48.2 Centiloids, respectively (p<0.001).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid CentiloidTau PETTreatment response monitoring

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13195-026-02163-9; NCT04437511

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Amyloid clearance at one year was most strongly related to starting amyloid burden, followed by age, APOE ε4 count and body weight. Clearance was associated with slower tau accumulation and a larger p-tau217 change, but clinical slowing was observed whether or not the PET threshold was reached. The analysis is exploratory and does not prove that forcing every patient below 24.1 Centiloids improves outcomes.

Study design

Investigators analyzed TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 randomized data (876 placebo; 860 donanemab) and an open-label addendum (1,053 participants). Donanemab-treated participants with evaluable week-52 PET were classified as amyloid-clear below 24.1 Centiloids or non-clear at 24.1 Centiloids or higher. Baseline predictors were assessed with machine learning and regression; propensity-matched placebo comparisons evaluated downstream biomarkers and clinical outcomes.

Key quantitative results

  • Among evaluable donanemab-treated participants, 443 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids at week 52 and 227 did not. Mean baseline amyloid was 95.8 versus 120.2 Centiloids; week-52 means were 4.8 versus 48.2 Centiloids, respectively (p<0.001).
  • Lower baseline amyloid was the most important predictor of clearance, followed by older age, fewer APOE ε4 alleles and lower body weight; baseline amyloid was inversely associated with clearance probability (p<0.001).
  • At week 76, only the amyloid-clear subgroup had significantly less tau accumulation than matched placebo (p<0.01). Both subgroups had significant plasma p-tau217 differences from matched placebo, with a larger change after clearance.
  • CDR-SB progression slowing versus matched placebo was 29.6% in the clear subgroup and 28.8% in the non-clear subgroup; iADRS slowing was 25.9% and 18.8%, respectively.

What changed

The analysis quantifies which baseline features predict one-year PET clearance and separates the relationship between clearance, downstream tau/p-tau217 change and clinical outcomes in a large phase 3 population.

Strength of evidence

Large trial-derived dataset with replication in an open-label addendum and quantitative PET, plasma and clinical outcomes. Causal interpretation is limited by post-hoc subgrouping, incomplete week-52 PET availability and propensity matching rather than randomized comparison between clearance states.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Starting amyloid burden influences the chance of crossing the 24.1-Centiloid threshold by one year. Failure to cross that threshold did not eliminate observed clinical slowing, so a single PET threshold should not be interpreted as an individual clinical-response rule without label- and pathway-specific evidence.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to MSL questions about PET monitoring, Centiloid thresholds, pharmacodynamic response, p-tau217 change, treatment duration and the distinction between amyloid clearance and patient benefit.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The analysis uses a prespecified quantitative amyloid-PET threshold of less than 24.1 Centiloids to define clearance. It supports Centiloid-based pharmacodynamic interpretation but does not validate visual reads, establish interchangeability across tracers or scanners, or authorize PET or plasma biomarkers as surrogate clinical end points.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, reimbursement or coverage change. Additional PET monitoring could carry cost and capacity implications, but this analysis did not establish a covered monitoring schedule.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did amyloid clearance predict a larger clinical benefit?
Not clearly. CDR-SB slowing was similar in clear and non-clear subgroups, while iADRS slowing was numerically larger after clearance; the post-hoc analysis was not randomized by clearance status.
Does 24.1 Centiloids become a validated surrogate end point?
No. The threshold operationalized PET clearance in this analysis; the study does not establish regulatory surrogacy or an individual stopping rule.
Was plasma p-tau217 sufficient to replace PET?
No. Plasma p-tau217 changed with treatment, but the study did not validate it as an interchangeable measure of PET clearance or clinical benefit.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Post-hoc exploratory subgroup analysis
  • Clearance status was not randomized
  • Only participants with evaluable week-52 PET entered the clearance comparison
  • Matched-placebo analyses may retain residual confounding
  • No new prospective monitoring algorithm or clinical-utility test

Primary source · DOI

Shcherbinin S, Lu M, Wang J, et al. Post-hoc analyses of amyloid reduction after one year of treatment with donanemab using clinical trial data: prediction of amyloid clearance and association with downstream measurements. Alzheimers Res Ther. Published online October 16, 2026. doi:10.1186/s13195-026-02163-9.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed multidisciplinary consensus recommendations•October 15, 2026

Italian intersocietal consensus specifies an anti-amyloid implementation pathway

Twenty-one Italian scientific societies and patient associations endorsed 36 operational statements that pair trial-aligned MRI eligibility and risk-adapted ARIA monitoring with a stepwise confirmation pathway using plasma biomarkers, automated CSF assays and amyloid PET.

Key recommendations: The panel evaluated 36 statements across five operational domains and reported strong agreement for the large majority.

BiomarkersGuidelinesManagementBloodAmyloidPlasma Alzheimer biomarkersBiological confirmation

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.tjpad.2026.100685; PMID:42880054

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The update translates European lecanemab and donanemab availability into a competence-based service model. It recommends harmonized CDR staging, a defined multidisciplinary team, trial-aligned MRI eligibility, risk-adapted ARIA monitoring and stepwise biomarker confirmation. Agreement was quantified through a modified Delphi process, but the source is consensus rather than a GRADE-based guideline or prospective utility study.

Evidence basis and population

After implementation gaps emerged from the panel's 2025 document, the Italian Expert Panel on Alzheimer reconvened 21 scientific societies and patient associations. A multidisciplinary panel rated 36 declarative statements across five domains: tiered cognitive-disorders services, clinical staging and monitoring, eligibility in MCI and atypical phenotypes, multidisciplinary-team composition, and MRI/ARIA/biomarker pathways.

Key recommendations

  • The panel evaluated 36 statements across five operational domains and reported strong agreement for the large majority.
  • The consensus recommends a competence-based reorganization of Italian cognitive-disorders centers and harmonized use of the Clinical Dementia Rating for staging and monitoring.
  • It endorses trial-aligned MRI eligibility criteria, a move toward risk-adapted ARIA monitoring, and a stepwise biomarker pathway integrating plasma assays, automated CSF platforms and amyloid PET.
  • The publication does not report formal GRADE certainty ratings or recommendation grades; its strength is quantified expert agreement from a modified Delphi process.

What changed

The Italian framework now addresses concrete operational gaps that appeared after European authorization, including how centers should be organized, how staging should be harmonized, and how blood, CSF, PET and MRI should be sequenced around treatment.

Strength of evidence

Multisociety consensus with a formal modified-Delphi method and broad stakeholder participation. Recommendations are operationally important but are not a substitute for drug labeling, national reimbursement rules, assay-specific validation or prospective clinical-utility evidence.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The document provides a practical blueprint for centers implementing anti-amyloid therapy in Italy, particularly for referral, confirmation, eligibility and ARIA surveillance. Local prescribing information and regional or national access rules remain controlling.

Field medical relevance

High value for MSL discussions about reflex testing, division of labor across laboratories and imaging services, atypical phenotypes, MRI thresholds, ARIA monitoring and the distinction between consensus, authorization and reimbursement.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The pathway is modality-specific but not product-specific: plasma tests are positioned within a stepwise pathway, automated CSF and amyloid PET provide biological confirmation, and MRI is used for eligibility and ARIA surveillance. The paper does not make assays or platforms interchangeable or establish new analytical-performance claims.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The framework is intended to support equitable and sustainable Italian access, but it does not itself create reimbursement, expand authorized indications or guarantee laboratory, PET or MRI capacity.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this a formal clinical practice guideline?
No. It is a final peer-reviewed intersocietal consensus produced with a modified Delphi process; the paper does not report GRADE-based recommendation strength.
Does it authorize plasma biomarkers as a stand-alone treatment test?
No. Plasma assays are incorporated into a stepwise pathway alongside automated CSF testing and amyloid PET, with clinical and imaging eligibility assessment still required.
Does it change reimbursement?
No. It offers a blueprint for prescribing centers and reimbursing authorities but is not itself a reimbursement or coverage decision.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Consensus rather than prospective implementation or outcomes evidence
  • Italian health-system context limits direct transfer to other jurisdictions
  • No formal GRADE certainty or recommendation-strength labels reported
  • Assay-specific cutoffs and analytical-performance requirements are not established by the consensus
  • Drug labels and payer rules remain separate

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Benussi A, Agosta F, Agnello L, et al. Updated Italian intersocietal recommendations for the appropriate use of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies in Alzheimer's disease. J Prev Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 15, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.tjpad.2026.100685.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed anatomical-phantom technical validation•October 15, 2026

An anatomical phantom exposes material bias in uncorrected amyloid-PET quantification

Across simulated gray-to-white matter ratios, uncorrected amyloid-PET measures had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% for tissue ratio and 19.8% for SUVR; partial-volume correction reduced them as low as 6.1% and 7.6%, with modified 3-compartment and GTM methods performing best.

Key quantitative results: Uncorrected gray-to-white ratio and SUVR had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% and 19.8%, respectively.

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid PET SUVRPET quantification

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s40658-026-00956-3

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Partial-volume effects can materially distort amyloid-PET SUVR, particularly when cortical atrophy or small structures mix gray and white matter signals. This phantom study shows that correction improves accuracy without a relevant loss of precision, but the best method still needs clinical validation on specific scanner, tracer and reconstruction combinations.

Study design

The StepBrain anatomical phantom was scanned to reproduce clinical amyloid-PET distributions across gray-to-white matter ratios from 0% to 120%. Atlas-based gray-to-white ratios and cerebellum-normalized SUVRs were calculated without correction and after 2-compartment, 3-compartment, modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix correction. Linear mixed models compared accuracy and precision against the known phantom ground truth.

Key quantitative results

  • Uncorrected gray-to-white ratio and SUVR had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% and 19.8%, respectively.
  • Partial-volume correction reduced mean absolute inaccuracy as low as 6.1% for gray-to-white ratio and 7.6% for SUVR.
  • Accuracy and precision differed significantly among methods for both measures (F>95 for all comparisons).
  • Three-compartment, modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix correction improved tracer-ratio accuracy without relevant precision loss; modified 3-compartment and GTM were the most accurate and precise.

What changed

The study supplies a physical ground truth for comparing amyloid-PET partial-volume methods and quantifies how much uncorrected SUVR can be biased in clinically realistic uptake patterns.

Strength of evidence

Strong analytical-method evidence within a controlled phantom experiment, with direct ground truth and head-to-head methods. Clinical validity and utility remain unproven because a phantom cannot reproduce motion, biological heterogeneity, tracer kinetics, scanner diversity or patient-specific anatomy.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Quantitative amyloid-PET reports should identify whether and how partial-volume correction was applied, especially for longitudinal monitoring or low-burden decisions. The numerical results should not be used as a universal correction factor.

Field medical relevance

Useful for MSL and imaging discussions about SUVR bias, atrophy, longitudinal treatment monitoring, method harmonization and why quantitative pipelines require scanner- and tracer-specific validation.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The head-to-head phantom comparison provides a known ground truth for partial-volume bias. Modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix approaches were most accurate and precise in this setup, but results do not establish universal equivalence across scanners, reconstructions, tracers, atlases or patient anatomy.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No access or coverage change. More advanced correction may require software, expertise and harmonized quality control that are not uniformly available.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Should every amyloid PET scan use the best-performing method from this study?
Not automatically. Modified 3-compartment and GTM performed best in this phantom, but each clinical pipeline needs validation for its tracer, scanner, reconstruction, atlas and patient population.
Does partial-volume correction eliminate bias?
No. It reduced mean absolute inaccuracy substantially but did not reduce it to zero.
Was clinical utility tested?
No. The study measured technical accuracy and precision, not diagnostic decisions, treatment selection or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Phantom rather than patient data
  • Does not reproduce motion, biological heterogeneity or tracer kinetics
  • Single experimental imaging and processing setup
  • No clinical decision thresholds or outcomes
  • No authorization, guideline or coverage assessment

Primary source · DOI

Pirozzi MA, Di Giorgio E, Prinster A, et al. Application of an anatomical brain phantom in the evaluation of partial volume effect correction of amyloid PET studies. EJNMMI Phys. Published online October 15, 2026. doi:10.1186/s40658-026-00956-3.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed randomized clinical trial•October 13, 2026

Low-intensity resource referral misses its caregiver self-efficacy endpoint

In a single-blind randomized trial, CommunityRx-Dementia did not improve 12-month caregiver self-efficacy or most prespecified outcomes among 133 caregivers with health-related social risks, although emergency-department use was lower (IRR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19-0.90).

Key quantitative results: Among caregivers with health-related social risks, 12-month self-efficacy was 3.5 in both groups (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30-2.09), so the primary endpoint was not met.

Clinical TrialsManagementCaregiver support

Added October 14, 2026 · DOI:10.1111/jgs.70684; PMID:42869650; NCT04146545

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

A personalized community-resource list, text-based navigation and online finder did not improve the trial's primary caregiver self-efficacy outcome in the prespecified higher-need group. Lower emergency-department use is clinically interesting but was one of several secondary outcomes and needs replication. The result argues against assuming that high engagement with a low-intensity referral service translates into broad caregiver benefit.

Study design

English-speaking dementia caregivers living in 62 ZIP codes around one urban academic medical center were randomized to usual care or usual care plus CommunityRx-Dementia. The intervention supplied education about common needs, a personalized list of nearby resources, text access to a navigator and an online resource finder. The prespecified primary analysis included 133 caregivers with at least one baseline health-related social risk; a post hoc analysis included 210 caregivers without such risks. Outcomes were assessed at 12 months.

Key quantitative results

  • Among caregivers with health-related social risks, 12-month self-efficacy was 3.5 in both groups (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30-2.09), so the primary endpoint was not met.
  • Loneliness was 41% versus 50% (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.24-1.59), needing help 23% versus 34% (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.30-2.11) and hospitalizations 0.1 versus 0.2 (IRR 0.42, 95% CI 0.14-1.30); none differed significantly.
  • Emergency-department utilization was lower with the intervention, 0.3 versus 0.7 visits (IRR 0.41, 95% CI 0.19-0.90). In the post hoc subgroup without baseline social risks, most outcomes were similar, while odds of needing help were lower (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12-0.83).
  • Engagement was high: 94% of caregivers with social risks texted a navigator and 31% requested additional resource information.

What changed

A completed randomized trial now provides controlled evidence that a scalable, low-intensity community-resource referral can achieve high engagement but does not by itself improve broad caregiver self-efficacy; its emergency-use signal remains secondary and exploratory for implementation decisions.

Strength of evidence

Moderate randomized evidence for the null primary outcome, with prespecified analysis and 12-month follow-up. Confidence in the emergency-department finding is lower because it was one of several secondary outcomes, event counts were self-reported, confidence intervals for other utilization outcomes were wide and the study was limited to one urban region.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Health systems should not present resource referral alone as a proven way to improve caregiver self-efficacy. The lower emergency-use signal may justify a larger implementation trial with verified utilization and prespecified multiplicity control, especially among caregivers facing social risks.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to caregiver-support program design, social-care navigation, health-equity implementation and discussions about which outcomes a low-touch intervention can reasonably change.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The intervention was designed to connect caregivers with local resources, but the study did not establish service availability outside the trial geography, reimbursement, scalable navigator capacity or coverage. Any reduction in access barriers remains unproven as a system-level outcome.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did CommunityRx-Dementia meet its primary endpoint?
No. Twelve-month caregiver self-efficacy was 3.5 in both groups, with OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.30-2.09).
Does the emergency-department result establish reduced acute-care use?
Not yet. It was a favorable secondary result based on self-report and should be confirmed in a larger trial using adjudicated utilization data.
Does the trial support reimbursement or a formal care standard?
No. It supplies intervention evidence but no guideline endorsement, payment decision or standardized implementation requirement.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single urban academic-center geography and English-speaking text-message users
  • Primary analysis included only 133 caregivers with baseline social risks
  • Emergency visits and hospitalizations were self-reported
  • Multiple secondary outcomes and a post hoc lower-risk subgroup
  • The primary endpoint and most prespecified secondary outcomes were null
  • No evidence of long-term sustainability, cost-effectiveness or reimbursement

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · ClinicalTrials.gov record

Makelarski JA, Wroblewski KE, Winslow VA, et al. Low-Intensity Social Care for Dementia Caregivers: A Randomized Trial. J Am Geriatr Soc. Published online October 13, 2026. doi:10.1111/jgs.70684.

Early signal•Peer-reviewed retrospective technical validation study•October 13, 2026

Quantitative MRI plus local language models drafts neurodegenerative reports

In 192 ADNI cases, an automated MRI-to-report pipeline achieved 77.6%-97.9% accuracy for CSF-space findings and 91.7%-97.4% agreement within one grade on ordinal visual scales, but strict scale agreement was only 27.1%-57.8% and no clinical utility was tested.

Key quantitative results: Accuracy for CSF-space analysis ranged from 77.6% to 97.9% across findings.

BiomarkersMRIBrain atrophyWhite matter hyperintensitiesImaging interpretation

Added October 14, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.acra.2026.09.056; PMID:42864178

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study separates quantitative extraction from narrative drafting and shows where each fails. CSF-space findings and one-grade-tolerant ordinal ratings were often close to neuroradiologist reports, but exact ordinal agreement was poor and model-specific omissions, additions and numeric errors persisted. This is feasibility evidence for reporting assistance, not validation for diagnosis, treatment eligibility or unsupervised use.

Study design

Investigators randomly selected 192 ADNI participants with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI. A deep-learning quantitative MRI system generated structured findings for nine indices covering atrophy, white matter hyperintensities and CSF-space abnormalities, which were compared with neuroradiologist reference reports. Four locally deployable language models—GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B—then drafted clinician-facing conclusions. Reviewers scored accuracy, relevance, clarity and satisfaction on five-point scales and categorized language, omission, addition and numeric errors.

Key quantitative results

  • Accuracy for CSF-space analysis ranged from 77.6% to 97.9% across findings.
  • For ordinal visual scales, strict agreement with reference reports was 27.1%-57.8%; allowing a one-grade difference increased agreement to 91.7%-97.4%.
  • GPT-OSS 20B achieved median Likert scores of 5 across most report-quality metrics and the lowest output-error rates. Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B had more language, omission and addition errors, while MedGemma had the highest numeric-error rate.
  • The study reported no prospective effect on neuroradiologist efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, downstream management or patient outcomes.

What changed

A new end-to-end evaluation quantifies both imaging-marker extraction and language-model drafting errors, providing a more operational test of automated neurodegenerative MRI reporting than standalone image-classification or text-generation studies.

Strength of evidence

Early technical feasibility evidence from a modest, retrospectively selected ADNI sample with neuroradiologist reports as the reference. The study does not establish analytical validity across scanners and sites, clinical validity against pathology or outcomes, or clinical utility in a prospective reporting workflow.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The pipeline may support structured drafting under neuroradiologist supervision, but low strict agreement on ordinal scales and model-specific numeric or content errors preclude autonomous interpretation. It should not be used to confirm Alzheimer pathology, stage disease or determine disease-modifying treatment eligibility without validated clinical review.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to biomarker implementation, radiology workflow design and MSL questions about how quantitative imaging and generative AI might standardize reporting while preserving human oversight.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Performance depended on the reporting component: GPT-OSS 20B achieved the highest overall ratings and lowest error rates, while smaller models produced more language, omission and addition errors and MedGemma had the highest numeric-error rate. The study did not validate interchangeability across models or scanners.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No availability, authorization, reimbursement or coverage change. Local language models could eventually reduce data-transfer barriers, but the study did not evaluate deployment cost, integration, governance, cybersecurity or access in routine practice.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the system match neuroradiologists exactly?
Not reliably for ordinal scales: strict agreement was 27.1%-57.8%. Agreement exceeded 91% only when a one-grade difference was accepted.
Was clinical utility demonstrated?
No. The study did not prospectively test report turnaround, diagnostic decisions, treatment selection, clinician behavior or patient outcomes.
Is the pipeline authorized for clinical use?
No authorization, guideline endorsement, availability or coverage was established in the report.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective sample of 192 ADNI participants
  • Reference was clinical reporting rather than pathology or an external outcome
  • Low strict agreement for ordinal visual scales
  • No external multi-site or scanner validation reported
  • Model-specific omissions, additions, language errors and numeric errors
  • No prospective workflow, clinical-utility or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Ko JS, Jung W, Suh PS, et al. Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models. Acad Radiol. Published online October 13, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.acra.2026.09.056.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective diagnostic and staging study•October 8, 2026

M-ACE supports rapid functional staging across the AD continuum

In 1,834 consecutive patients, the Mini-Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination closely tracked the full ACE-III (ρ=0.822), outperformed MMSE at the subjective-decline-to-MCI transition and yielded stage-specific cutoffs, but retrospective FAST-based classification does not establish etiologic Alzheimer diagnosis or treatment eligibility.

Key quantitative results: M-ACE showed good internal consistency (McDonald's ω=0.835; Cronbach's α=0.731) and strong convergence with ACE-III (Spearman ρ=0.822).

ManagementCognitive screening

Added October 8, 2026 · DOI:10.5603/pjnns.113649; PMID:42841817

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This large clinic cohort gives M-ACE a more specific role than generic screening: rapid follow-up and functional-stage discrimination, particularly early in the continuum. ACE-III remained the most consistently accurate instrument across transitions, while M-ACE lost discrimination later as memory recall reached a floor. The cutoffs are cohort-derived aids, not standalone diagnoses, biomarker substitutes or prescribing thresholds.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively analyzed 1,834 consecutive people seeking cognitive evaluation and classified them as subjective cognitive decline (FAST 2), mild cognitive impairment (FAST 3) or Alzheimer dementia (FAST 4-6). They compared M-ACE, ACE-III and MMSE using reliability, convergent validity, ROC analyses, optimal cutoffs, DeLong tests and stage-adjusted logistic regression.

Key quantitative results

  • M-ACE showed good internal consistency (McDonald's ω=0.835; Cronbach's α=0.731) and strong convergence with ACE-III (Spearman ρ=0.822).
  • M-ACE significantly outperformed MMSE for the FAST 2-to-3 transition and remained independently associated with stage after adjustment for age, sex and education. ACE-III had the most consistently high accuracy across transitions; MMSE had the highest AUC at FAST 4-to-5, but not significantly higher than ACE-III.
  • Optimal M-ACE cutoffs were ≤25 for FAST 2-to-3, ≤19 for FAST 3-to-4, ≤13 for FAST 4-to-5 and ≤7 for FAST 5-to-6. Memory Recall developed a floor effect from FAST 4, helping explain M-ACE's weaker late-stage discrimination.

What changed

The study supplies a large, stage-specific comparison of M-ACE, ACE-III and MMSE and proposes operational M-ACE thresholds for rapid longitudinal follow-up across the functional Alzheimer continuum.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence for functional-stage discrimination in the studied referral cohort: large consecutive sample, direct instrument comparison and adjusted analyses are strengths. Retrospective design, cohort-derived cutoffs and FAST-based classification limit causal interpretation, external transportability and use for etiologic diagnosis.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

M-ACE may be a practical short instrument for repeated cognitive assessment when a full ACE-III is not feasible, especially around the subjective-decline-to-MCI transition. It should complement history, function, neurologic evaluation and indicated biomarker testing rather than determine an Alzheimer etiology or disease-modifying-treatment eligibility alone.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to memory-clinic workflow, stage documentation and selection of brief follow-up tools. It also reinforces the distinction between cognitive/functional staging and biological confirmation of Alzheimer pathology.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The study creates no new test authorization, commercial availability, guideline endorsement, reimbursement or coverage. M-ACE is a cognitive instrument; local licensing, language validation, training and workflow determine implementation.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can the proposed M-ACE cutoffs diagnose Alzheimer disease?
No. They discriminate FAST transitions in this retrospective clinical cohort. They do not establish Alzheimer etiology or replace amyloid confirmation when treatment or another decision requires it.
Is M-ACE better than ACE-III?
Not overall. ACE-III was the most consistently accurate across stages. M-ACE offered a useful balance of speed and accuracy, particularly at earlier transitions and for follow-up.
Does this change authorization, endorsement or coverage?
No. It is a performance study, not a regulatory action, formal guideline or payer decision.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-system clinical cohort
  • Stage classification was based on FAST rather than a uniform biomarker reference standard
  • Cutoffs were derived in the same clinical population and need external validation
  • The public report does not establish prospective management or patient-outcome benefit
  • M-ACE memory recall showed a floor effect from FAST stage 4
  • Results do not define anti-amyloid treatment eligibility

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Barczak A, Golan MP, Hintze B. Comparative diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of the Mini-Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination, ACE-III, and MMSE for functional staging across the Alzheimer's disease continuum. Neurol Neurochir Pol. Published online October 8, 2026. doi:10.5603/pjnns.113649.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed dynamic microsimulation and health-economic analysis•October 7, 2026

Model quantifies value lost when anti-amyloid treatment is delayed

A U.S. microsimulation projected $104,885 in gross lifetime societal value per treated person and 32% more value when anti-amyloid treatment began two years earlier, but these are model-based gross benefits that exclude drug, screening and monitoring costs.

Key quantitative results: Treatment generated $104,885 in gross lifetime societal value per person (95% CI $99,291-$110,479), including quality-of-life gains, reduced unpaid caregiving and medical cost offsets driven largely by less nursing-home use and Medicaid spending.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment access

Added October 8, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/alz.71819; PMID:42841389; PMCID:PMC13643942

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The model reframes diagnostic delay as potential loss of health, independence, caregiver time and public-program savings. Earlier treatment consistently improved projected value, but the headline figures are gross societal benefits—not cost-effectiveness ratios—and omit the costs required to find, confirm, infuse and monitor eligible patients. Results depend on assumptions about durability and whether earlier-stage efficacy is stronger.

Study design

Using a U.S. dynamic microsimulation, investigators modeled people resembling an early symptomatic Alzheimer trial population (mean baseline age 73.0 years). A treatment scenario slowed clinical progression by 29% over the remaining lifetime; an earlier scenario initiated therapy two years sooner. Outcomes included survival, disability-free time, community residence, quality of life, unpaid caregiving and medical spending, with sensitivity analyses for stronger early-stage efficacy and four-year effect duration.

Key quantitative results

  • Treatment generated $104,885 in gross lifetime societal value per person (95% CI $99,291-$110,479), including quality-of-life gains, reduced unpaid caregiving and medical cost offsets driven largely by less nursing-home use and Medicaid spending.
  • Starting treatment two years earlier increased modeled value by 32%. When the model also assumed 36% rather than 29% slowing in earlier disease, value was 71% higher than the trial-timing scenario.
  • With treatment benefit limited to four years, gross lifetime value fell to $49,122 for trial-timing treatment and $56,385 for earlier treatment. The model projected about 0.3 additional life-years, 1.0 fewer year with severe dementia, 0.37 disability-free years and 0.63 additional years in the community for the trial-timing treatment scenario.

What changed

A new U.S. model quantifies the potential societal cost of diagnostic and treatment delay and provides sensitivity ranges that health systems can compare with the real costs of screening, confirmation, infusion and monitoring.

Strength of evidence

Moderate modeling evidence for directional and scenario-based planning, grounded in trial efficacy and national data but not a prospective outcome or cost-effectiveness study. Conclusions are assumption-sensitive, particularly to duration of benefit, earlier-stage efficacy, treatment uptake and excluded implementation costs.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support reducing avoidable diagnostic and treatment delays for otherwise eligible patients, while underscoring that implementation decisions require the omitted drug, biomarker, imaging, infusion, staffing and safety costs. The model should not be used to promise an individual benefit or to broaden treatment beyond labeled populations.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to access strategy, diagnostic-pathway investment, payer and health-system value discussions, and MSL questions about why earlier identification may matter even when clinical-trial efficacy is fixed.

Access or reimbursement relevance

High contextual relevance but no access action. The study quantifies potential value from shorter diagnostic and treatment delays; it does not establish coverage, reimbursement, capacity, assay availability or a funded care pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is $104,885 the net value after treatment costs?
No. It is gross societal value. Drug acquisition, diagnostic testing, infusions, MRI monitoring and implementation costs were not subtracted.
Does the model prove that every patient benefits more if treated two years earlier?
No. It projects population-average outcomes under specified assumptions and does not replace individual eligibility, risk-benefit assessment or observed clinical data.
Does this change coverage or eligibility?
No. It supplies an economic benchmark; FDA labeling, clinical guidance and payer coverage remain separate.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Microsimulation rather than prospective comparative outcomes
  • Gross value excludes drug, screening, biomarker, infusion and monitoring costs
  • Relies on assumed lifetime or four-year persistence of treatment effect
  • Earlier-stage efficacy scenarios are modeled rather than directly randomized
  • Results reflect U.S. costs, caregiving and Medicaid structures
  • Industry-related institutional funding and author relationships are disclosed

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Chapel JM, Tysinger B, Pourmand H, Goldman D, Aisen P; Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. The value of timely treatment with anti-amyloid therapy for Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimers Dement. 2026;22(10):e71819. doi:10.1002/alz.71819.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed prospective cohort study•October 7, 2026

Sweet-tooth preference tracks with higher dementia risk

In a prospective UK Biobank analysis, a sweet-tooth preference profile was associated with 79% higher all-cause dementia risk, 62% higher Alzheimer disease risk and 202% higher vascular-dementia risk than a health-aligned profile; the observational design does not show that changing preference prevents dementia.

Key quantitative results: Compared with the health-aligned profile, the sweet-tooth profile was associated with 79% higher all-cause dementia risk, 62% higher Alzheimer disease risk and 202% higher vascular-dementia risk.

ManagementRisk reduction

Added October 8, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s11357-026-02567-3; PMID:42842075

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study links a preference for sweet foods—not measured intake—to future dementia and to three biological-aging measures, with stronger joint risk among people with high genetic susceptibility. The effect sizes are sizeable, but residual confounding, selection, reverse causation and imperfect translation from preference to consumption prevent causal or prescriptive claims. Biological-aging markers explained only a small share of the association.

Study design

Investigators used UK Biobank food-preference questionnaires to derive health-aligned, broad-preference and sweet-tooth profiles by latent profile analysis. Cox models related profiles to incident all-cause, Alzheimer and vascular dementia and tested interaction with genetic risk. Linear models assessed KDM biological-age acceleration, PhenoAge acceleration and leukocyte telomere length; mediation analyses were exploratory.

Key quantitative results

  • Compared with the health-aligned profile, the sweet-tooth profile was associated with 79% higher all-cause dementia risk, 62% higher Alzheimer disease risk and 202% higher vascular-dementia risk.
  • The sweet-tooth profile was also associated with faster Klemera-Doubal biological-age and PhenoAge acceleration and shorter leukocyte telomere length. A significant additive interaction indicated greater combined dementia risk with high genetic susceptibility.
  • Exploratory mediation analyses estimated that the three biological-aging measures statistically accounted for only 2.28%-4.82% of the observed diet-preference association, leaving most of the association unexplained.

What changed

The cohort adds prospective, profile-based evidence connecting sweet-food preference, genetic susceptibility, multiple biological-aging measures and dementia subtypes in one analysis.

Strength of evidence

Moderate observational evidence for association, supported by prospective follow-up, time-to-event analysis and convergent aging measures. It is insufficient for causality or a treatment recommendation because exposure was preference rather than intake, confounding and reverse causation remain possible, and mediation was exploratory.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings are consistent with counseling toward established healthy dietary patterns as part of multidomain risk reduction, but they do not justify genetic testing, a sweet-food cutoff or a claim that changing food preferences will prevent Alzheimer disease.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to risk-reduction discussions and prevention-study design, particularly questions about diet-genetic interaction and whether biological-aging measures explain dementia associations.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The study creates no authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, reimbursement or coverage change. Its implications concern prevention research and counseling context rather than access to a specific product or service.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does a sweet tooth cause Alzheimer disease?
The study shows association, not causation. Food preference is not the same as measured intake, and unmeasured confounding or preclinical disease could contribute.
Should APOE or polygenic testing be ordered to target dietary counseling?
No clinical-testing recommendation follows from this observational interaction analysis. Risk counseling should rely on established guidance and individual context.
Did biological aging explain most of the association?
No. The exploratory mediators accounted for only 2.28%-4.82%, so most of the association was not explained by those measures.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Observational UK Biobank design with healthy-volunteer selection
  • Food preference rather than objectively measured consumption
  • Residual confounding and reverse causation cannot be excluded
  • Genetic interaction and mediation analyses do not establish clinical utility
  • Biological-aging measures explained only a small proportion of the association
  • No randomized evidence that changing preference reduces dementia incidence

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Sun M, Huang F, Sun N, et al. Dietary preference, biological aging, and incident dementia: a prospective cohort study. Geroscience. Published online October 7, 2026. doi:10.1007/s11357-026-02567-3.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed prospective randomized clinical-utility trial•October 5, 2026

Earlier blood-biomarker disclosure raises certainty and changes care

In the 220-person PLASMAR randomized trial, disclosing plasma p-tau217 and NfL at three rather than nine months increased very high-confidence etiologic diagnoses from 4.6% to 50.0% and advanced several management decisions without worse anxiety, depression or quality of life.

Key quantitative results: At three months, 56/112 participants (50.0%) in the earlier-disclosure arm versus 5/108 (4.6%) in the delayed-disclosure arm had a very high-confidence etiologic diagnosis (p<0.001). After both groups received results, certainty converged: 56/112 (50.0%) after early disclosure versus 57/108 (52.8%) after delayed disclosure (p=0.68).

BiomarkersClinical TrialsBloodp-tau217NfLEtiologic diagnosis

Added October 6, 2026 · NCT06246019; DOI:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.3497; PMID:42832237

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

PLASMAR supplies randomized evidence for clinical utility rather than another accuracy estimate. Earlier p-tau217/NfL disclosure made clinicians more certain and moved treatment, cognitive-stimulation and follow-up plans forward. The result is strongest at low and high p-tau217 likelihoods, not intermediate results, and it does not prove better cognition, function, long-term outcomes or value in primary care.

Study design

A public-hospital memory clinic in Barcelona randomized 220 consecutive new outpatients with subjective cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia and no prior etiologic diagnosis to disclosure of plasma p-tau217 and NfL at three months (n=112) or nine months (n=108). The prespecified primary outcome was a clinician-rated etiologic diagnosis with at least 90% confidence at three months; secondary outcomes included diagnosis changes, treatment and follow-up decisions, and patient-reported emotional outcomes through approximately nine months.

Key quantitative results

  • At three months, 56/112 participants (50.0%) in the earlier-disclosure arm versus 5/108 (4.6%) in the delayed-disclosure arm had a very high-confidence etiologic diagnosis (p<0.001). After both groups received results, certainty converged: 56/112 (50.0%) after early disclosure versus 57/108 (52.8%) after delayed disclosure (p=0.68).
  • Earlier disclosure increased symptomatic AD-treatment initiation to 16/112 (14.3%) versus 5/108 (4.6%), an absolute difference of 9.7 percentage points (95% CI 1.8 to 17.8; p=0.01), and cognitive-stimulation referral to 51/112 (45.5%) versus 33/108 (30.6%; p=0.03).
  • Planned neuropsychological reassessment was lower with earlier disclosure (34/112 [30.4%] vs 57/108 [52.8%]; difference −22.4 points, 95% CI −34.4 to −9.4; p<0.001), while planned discharge to primary care was higher (35/112 [31.3%] vs 13/108 [12.0%]; difference 19.2 points, 95% CI 8.4 to 29.5; p<0.001). Anxiety/depression and quality-of-life changes did not differ between groups.

What changed

The field gained randomized evidence that the timing of blood-biomarker disclosure can causally change diagnostic certainty and near-term clinical management in a memory-clinic pathway, extending beyond observational pre/post implementation studies.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-high evidence for short-term clinical utility in the studied pathway: randomized design, prespecified primary outcome and intention-to-treat analysis support causality. Generalizability and downstream benefit remain limited by one center, nine-month follow-up, attrition, incomplete CSF/PET reference testing and multiple secondary comparisons without multiplicity adjustment.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The trial supports timely, structured disclosure of decisive p-tau217/NfL results in specialty memory care and suggests that low-likelihood results may reduce prolonged diagnostic follow-up. It does not show that earlier disclosure improves cognition, function, quality of life, long-term outcomes or disease-modifying treatment access.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to MSL questions about clinical utility, result disclosure, dual-cutoff interpretation, diagnostic confidence and downstream workflow. It also clarifies why analytical validity, clinical validity, clinical utility, authorization, guideline endorsement and coverage must be assessed separately.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The trial evaluated a p-tau217/NfL disclosure pathway rather than comparative assay performance. Its utility findings should not be assumed to transfer unchanged across platforms, cutoffs or reporting formats.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The publication establishes neither assay authorization nor routine availability, guideline endorsement, reimbursement or payer coverage. Costs, capacity, equity and disease-modifying-treatment access were not evaluated.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this trial validate p-tau217 analytical performance or diagnostic accuracy?
No. It tested clinical utility of disclosing p-tau217 and NfL together. Not all participants received CSF or amyloid PET, and analytical validation was not the research question.
Did earlier disclosure improve patient outcomes?
It improved short-term diagnostic certainty and changed management plans, but the trial did not demonstrate better cognition, function, quality of life or disease course.
Were intermediate p-tau217 results equally useful?
No. Very high confidence at three months was 1/13 with early disclosure versus 2/18 with delayed disclosure in the intermediate group; the utility signal was concentrated in low- and high-likelihood results.
Does the report establish authorization, availability, endorsement or coverage?
No. It is a clinical-utility trial from one Spanish memory clinic, not a regulatory, commercial-availability, guideline or payer action.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single public-hospital memory clinic in Spain
  • p-tau217 and NfL were disclosed together, so independent contributions cannot be separated
  • Not all participants had CSF or amyloid PET reference testing
  • Secondary analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons
  • Some management outcomes were clinician-reported intended plans rather than mandated completed actions
  • Approximately nine months of follow-up with attrition in questionnaire analyses
  • Disease-modifying therapy was not routinely available in the study setting

Primary source · DOI · ClinicalTrials.gov record · PubMed record

Estragués-Gázquez I, Contador J, Martínez LD, et al. Earlier Disclosure of Blood-Based Biomarkers, Diagnostic Certainty, and Clinical Management: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Neurol. Published online October 5, 2026. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.3497.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective clinical-validity and discordance study•October 1, 2026

Clinical context helps explain definite-zone p-tau217 discordance

Among 706 Mayo Clinic patients with plasma p-tau217 outside the intermediate zone and confirmatory amyloid PET and/or CSF, 60 (8.5%) were discordant: false negatives were more common than false positives (5.6% vs 2.8%; p=0.007), with disease stage, kidney function, body mass index and obstructive sleep apnea associated with discordance patterns.

Key quantitative results: Sixty of 706 patients (8.5%) had discordant results. False negatives occurred in 5.6% and false positives in 2.8% (p=0.007). Across both discordance types, older age was associated with discordance (OR 1.61 per decade; 95% CI 1.23–2.14), as was obstructive sleep apnea (OR 1.94; 95% CI 1.08–3.49).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217AmyloidBiological confirmation

Added October 2, 2026 · DOI:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218591; PMID:42821845

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Definite-zone p-tau217 results agreed with established amyloid measures in most patients, but discordance was not random. False negatives clustered with milder clinical stage, higher body mass index, better kidney function and obstructive sleep apnea; false positives clustered with older age, lower kidney function and more advanced impairment. These are signals for confirmatory testing and contextual interpretation, not post hoc permission to relabel a discordant result or use the associations as correction factors.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively identified 706 Mayo Clinic patients whose plasma p-tau217 was definitely positive (>0.324 pg/mL) or definitely negative (<0.186 pg/mL) and who had an amyloid PET and/or CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 result. They classified plasma results as true positive, true negative, false positive or false negative against the established biomarker result and modeled demographic, clinical, comorbidity and laboratory factors associated with discordance.

Key quantitative results

  • Sixty of 706 patients (8.5%) had discordant results. False negatives occurred in 5.6% and false positives in 2.8% (p=0.007). Across both discordance types, older age was associated with discordance (OR 1.61 per decade; 95% CI 1.23–2.14), as was obstructive sleep apnea (OR 1.94; 95% CI 1.08–3.49).
  • Compared with true positives, false negatives had higher MMSE scores (OR 1.20 per point), more obstructive sleep apnea (OR 2.01), higher body mass index (OR 1.11 per kg/m²) and higher estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR 1.33 per 10 mL/min/1.73 m²). Age-adjusted analyses retained body mass index (OR 1.14), estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR 1.63) and earlier Clinical Dementia Rating stage as associations.
  • Compared with true negatives, false positives were associated with older age (OR 2.37 per decade), thyroid disease (OR 4.41), lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (OR 0.48 per 10 mL/min/1.73 m²) and more advanced Clinical Dementia Rating stage. In age-adjusted analyses, estimated glomerular filtration rate remained associated (OR 0.54), while CDR ≥1 carried OR 11.11 versus CDR 0 and OR 4.55 versus CDR 0.5.

What changed

An October 1 Neurology report quantifies the residual discordance within definite plasma p-tau217 zones and identifies clinical patterns that can guide when a seemingly definitive result still warrants adjudication with PET, CSF or broader diagnostic evaluation.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity and interpretation evidence from a 706-patient specialty-center cohort with established-biomarker comparators. Associations are observational, several subgroups are small, the reference standard combines PET and CSF, and the public abstract does not establish prospective decision impact or transportability to other assays and settings.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A definite plasma result should be interpreted alongside clinical stage and kidney function, with attention to obesity and obstructive sleep apnea when the phenotype and biomarker disagree. The findings support targeted confirmation rather than automatic acceptance or mathematical adjustment of the plasma value.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to blood-biomarker triage, discordant-result workups, specialty referral, pretest counseling and communication about why two-cutoff algorithms reduce but do not eliminate uncertainty.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study used an assay-specific two-cutoff plasma p-tau217 workflow, with definite negative below 0.186 pg/mL and definite positive above 0.324 pg/mL. The public abstract does not name the assay platform; the cutoffs and associations should not be transferred to other products, matrices or workflows without validation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, guideline or coverage change occurred. The study may improve selection for confirmatory testing, but payer requirements and product-specific intended uses remain unchanged.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does 8.5% mean the test was only 91.5% accurate?
Not necessarily. The cohort included only definite-zone plasma results with PET and/or CSF confirmation, and the analysis focused on discordance rather than a population-screening accuracy estimate. Prevalence, referral patterns and the combined reference standard affect the observed proportion.
Should kidney function or body mass index be used to correct p-tau217 values?
No correction equation was validated. These variables identify contexts in which discordance was more likely and may justify confirmation; they do not establish a new adjusted cutoff.
Did the study establish clinical utility?
No. It supports clinical validity and contextual interpretation but did not test whether using these factors improves decisions, treatment eligibility, outcomes, safety or cost.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective specialty-center cohort
  • Observational associations cannot establish why discordance occurred
  • Amyloid PET and CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 were combined as the established-biomarker reference
  • Only 60 discordant cases, with smaller false-positive and false-negative subgroups
  • Public abstract does not name the assay platform or report external validation
  • No prospective decision-impact, treatment-access or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Shir D, Algeciras-Schimnich A, Piura YD, et al. Clinical factors associated with discordant plasma P-Tau217 and established Alzheimer disease biomarkers. Neurology. Published online October 1, 2026. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218591.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world imaging study•October 8, 2026

Real-world lecanemab PET monitoring reveals visual-quantitative discordance

In 38 amyloid-PET-positive patients treated for 6–8 months, amyloid burden fell by 29.39±22.31 Centiloids, but visual and quantitative response agreement was poor to fair (κ 0.205–0.253), supporting explicit Centiloid quantification for serial monitoring rather than visual interpretation alone.

Key quantitative results: Mean amyloid reduction was 29.39±22.31 Centiloids (p<0.001); MMSE, MoCA and tau-PET measures did not change significantly.

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid CentiloidTau PET SUVRTreatment response monitoring

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261493063

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The cohort shows substantial short-term plaque reduction without measurable cognitive or tau-PET change. Only 12 of 38 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids and five were visually negative. The discordance supports quantitative serial assessment when PET is obtained, but this small uncontrolled cohort cannot prove clinical utility or determine when treatment should stop.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively analyzed 38 amyloid-PET-positive patients with Alzheimer disease who received lecanemab for 6–8 months. Paired tests evaluated Centiloid and cognitive change, kappa measured visual-quantitative agreement, and exploratory regression assessed predictors of amyloid reduction.

Key quantitative results

  • Mean amyloid reduction was 29.39±22.31 Centiloids (p<0.001); MMSE, MoCA and tau-PET measures did not change significantly.
  • Twelve of 38 patients reached less than 24.1 Centiloids, while only five were visually negative.
  • Visual-quantitative agreement was poor to fair: κ=0.205 for positivity and κ=0.253 for treatment efficacy.
  • Baseline Centiloid burden (standardized β=0.594, p<0.001) and number of treatment cycles (β=0.285, p=0.022) independently predicted greater clearance; tau SUVR had a marginal inverse association (β=-0.238, p=0.052). The multivariable model adjusted R² was 0.507.

What changed

This real-world study directly quantifies the gap between visual and Centiloid-based interpretation during short-term lecanemab therapy and proposes a hybrid screening-and-monitoring workflow.

Strength of evidence

Early real-world evidence with paired PET and quantitative effect estimates, but retrospective, uncontrolled and limited to 38 patients. Visual-reading methods, tracer/scanner generalizability and downstream clinical utility require independent validation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

If serial amyloid PET is obtained, visual negativity alone may miss low residual burden and quantitative Centiloid reporting can add interpretive precision. The study does not establish that routine serial PET improves outcomes or should guide dose changes.

Field medical relevance

Addresses recurring MSL questions about visual versus quantitative reads, low-burden discordance, Centiloid thresholds and PET-based response monitoring under anti-amyloid therapy.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The central comparison is visual versus quantitative amyloid-PET interpretation during lecanemab treatment. Poor agreement indicates that visual and Centiloid assessments are not interchangeable near low residual burden; the study did not validate performance across tracers, scanners or independent readers.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization or coverage change. Serial quantitative PET could increase imaging demand and cost; the study did not evaluate reimbursement or access.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does the study establish routine serial PET monitoring?
No. It shows measurement discordance in a small cohort but did not test whether serial PET improves treatment decisions or outcomes.
Can visual negativity and less than 24.1 Centiloids be treated as equivalent?
No. Twelve patients crossed the quantitative threshold while only five were visually negative, and kappa agreement was low.
Did plaque reduction produce short-term cognitive improvement?
No significant MMSE or MoCA change was detected over 6–8 months.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly published item
  • Retrospective single-cohort design
  • Only 38 patients
  • No untreated comparator
  • Short 6–8-month follow-up
  • No validation across tracers, scanners or independent readers
  • No clinical-utility or patient-outcome analysis

Primary source · DOI

Qiao Z, Zhao X, Wang G, et al. PET-based evaluation of short-term amyloid-β clearance and predictive factors in real-world Alzheimer's disease patients treated with lecanemab. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 8, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261493063.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed autopsy-confirmed PET-pathology study•September 23, 2026

Autopsy validation shows late-stage flortaucipir uptake differs across primary cortex

Among 155 autopsy-confirmed Alzheimer cases, flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices began at Braak stage V, with visual and auditory regions increasing earlier and faster than motor and somatosensory regions.

Key quantitative results: The analysis included 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with Alzheimer disease.

BiomarkersTau PETFlortaucipir tau PETBraak neurofibrillary tangle stageBiological staging

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117530; PMID:42830961; PMCID:PMC13634365

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Primary isocortex is usually emphasized as the terminal Braak stage, but uptake was not uniform. Visual and auditory cortex showed earlier and steeper flortaucipir increases than motor and somatosensory cortex, and age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake. The result refines late-stage spatial interpretation without validating a new treatment-selection threshold.

Study design

Researchers measured flortaucipir uptake in primary visual, auditory, motor and somatosensory isocortices in 155 participants with autopsy-confirmed Alzheimer disease, then related regional uptake to neuropathologic Braak stage and clinical or genetic covariates.

Key quantitative results

  • The analysis included 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with Alzheimer disease.
  • Flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices became apparent beginning at Braak stage V.
  • Visual and auditory isocortices showed greater and faster uptake increases than somatosensory and motor cortex.
  • Age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake; primary-isocortex patterns resembled lateral temporal cortex more than entorhinal cortex.

What changed

The pathology-anchored analysis shows that primary cortical regions do not behave as one homogeneous late-stage tau-PET compartment and that visual/auditory regions may signal advanced spread earlier than traditionally emphasized.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence because diagnosis and Braak stage were autopsy confirmed and the cohort was sizeable for pathology studies. The analysis remains cross-sectional and tracer-specific, and clinical utility was not tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Regional late-stage flortaucipir interpretation may need to distinguish visual and auditory cortex from motor and somatosensory cortex. The findings do not create a new authorized stage, threshold or treatment-eligibility rule.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to tau-PET visual and quantitative staging, spatial reporting, pathology concordance and discussions of how late-stage regional uptake should be interpreted.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study links regional flortaucipir uptake to neuropathologically confirmed Braak stage. It supports regional interpretation for this tracer but does not establish equivalence with other tau tracers, visual-staging schemes or quantitative pipelines.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new availability or coverage change. The study may inform specialist interpretation but does not expand access to tau PET.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does uptake in primary cortex define a new clinical stage?
No. The study refines regional relationships with neuropathologic Braak stage but does not validate a new clinical staging system.
Can the pattern be generalized to every tau tracer?
No. The evidence is specific to flortaucipir and requires tracer-specific replication.
Was treatment eligibility or response tested?
No. This was a PET-pathology interpretation study.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly published item
  • Cross-sectional analysis
  • Tracer-specific findings
  • Potential interval between PET and autopsy
  • No prospective visual-reading or treatment-decision utility test

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Full text in PubMed Central

Josephs KA, Weigand SD, Satoh R, et al. Neurofibrillary tangle deposition in primary idiotypic isocortices using flortaucipir PET in histopathologically confirmed Alzheimer's disease. iScience. Published online September 23, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117530.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world diagnostic workflow study•October 2, 2026

Sequential Lumipulse testing reduced the p-tau217 indeterminate zone

In 562 consecutive memory-clinic patients, using the p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio only after an intermediate p-tau217 result reduced indeterminate classifications from 17.8% to 12.3% and was estimated to spare 56 confirmatory CSF or amyloid-PET tests per 1,000 patients.

Key quantitative results: Core 1 amyloid positivity was 71.2% (400/562); p-tau217 AUC was 0.935 (95% CI, 0.908-0.962).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42Triage

Added October 14, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13195-026-02218-x

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The practical message is about test sequencing, not simply which analyte has the highest AUC. A p-tau217-first pathway followed by the p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio only for intermediate results reduced unresolved cases while avoiding universal ratio testing. External validation and prospective decision-impact testing are still needed.

Study design

Retrospective analysis of 562 consecutive memory-clinic patients assessed from October 2023 through April 2026. Core 1 amyloid status used CSF biomarkers and/or amyloid PET. The study compared p-tau217 alone, universal upfront p-tau217/Aβ42, and a p-tau217-first reflex-ratio workflow using rule-out and rule-in thresholds selected for at least 95% sensitivity and specificity.

Key quantitative results

  • Core 1 amyloid positivity was 71.2% (400/562); p-tau217 AUC was 0.935 (95% CI, 0.908-0.962).
  • The p-tau217 two-threshold approach left 17.8% intermediate, with 94.1% accuracy in the decision zones.
  • Universal upfront p-tau217/Aβ42 improved AUC to 0.946 (p=0.011) but reduced indeterminacy only to 17.1%.
  • The sequential workflow reduced indeterminacy to 12.3%, with sensitivity 0.937, specificity 0.935, PPV 0.973, NPV 0.855, and 56 fewer confirmatory CSF or amyloid-PET tests per 1,000 patients.

What changed

The study tested where a plasma ratio adds operational value and found that targeted reflex use in the p-tau217 gray zone was more efficient than universal upfront ratio testing.

Strength of evidence

Moderate implementation evidence from a consecutive real-world cohort with internal temporal validation and a 15-percentage-point prevalence shift. It remains retrospective, single-center, and internally thresholded.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A reflex-ratio workflow may reduce unresolved plasma results and prioritize which patients need CSF or amyloid PET, but the numerical cutoffs should not be transferred to another population or platform without validation.

Field medical relevance

Useful for discussions about gray-zone management, reflex algorithms, why a small AUC gain may not translate into a large workflow gain, and the distinction between fewer confirmatory tests and proven patient benefit.

Quanterix or platform relevance

This is directly relevant to automated-platform positioning: the ratio added the most value as a reflex test for the p-tau217 intermediate zone rather than as an upfront replacement for every patient. The cutoffs remain cohort- and platform-specific.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The modeled pathway could reduce CSF or amyloid-PET use, but the study did not measure actual costs, reimbursement, access, or realized downstream utilization.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does the ratio replace p-tau217 as the first test?
Not in this study. Its largest operational benefit came when used only after an intermediate p-tau217 result.
Can these cutoffs be used in another laboratory?
No. They were selected and validated internally in one specialty-clinic cohort on the Lumipulse G600II.
Did the workflow improve patient outcomes?
No. It modeled diagnostic classification and confirmatory-test use; it did not prospectively test treatment decisions or outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center design
  • High specialty-clinic amyloid prevalence
  • Internally selected thresholds
  • CSF and/or PET composite reference
  • No prospective decision-impact or patient-outcome trial
